analysis.one_liner: Taxed oil futures trading to curb speculation and fund highways.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House tax committee after being referred on July 29, 2009, and received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have placed a small tax on each trade in oil futures and options — 0.2% of the value of a futures trade and 0.5% of the price of an option — to discourage rapid, speculative betting that pushes oil prices up and down. Trades by airlines, refiners, and other businesses that hedge real oil purchases would be exempt. The money raised would go into the Highway Trust Fund, which pays for road and transit projects.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and everyone who pays for gasoline, diesel, and goods shipped by road, through calmer oil prices and more money for highway repairs; road builders and state transportation programs would gain a new funding stream.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a 0.2% tax on oil futures trades and 0.5% on oil options, aimed at deterring short-term speculative trades that the bill's findings say drove oil price swings unconnected to supply and demand [S2] [S3].

Airlines, trucking firms, refiners, and other commercial traders making bona fide hedging transactions are explicitly exempt from the tax, so businesses buying oil for actual use would not pay it [S2] [S3].

All revenue from the tax would be deposited into the Highway Trust Fund, which funds road and highway programs — a stated fit because roughly 70% of U.S. oil consumption is for transportation [S2] [S3].
Withholding rules would apply the tax to foreign buyers of U.S. oil futures, closing the most obvious route around it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Speculative traders and the exchanges where oil futures are traded, which would pay or collect the tax on every transaction; to the extent the tax deters speculative trading, its cost is intended to fall on that activity rather than on oil consumers.

drawbacks.text: A transaction tax can push trading to foreign exchanges that the tax cannot reach, since the tax applies only to trades on U.S. trading facilities or by U.S. persons; trading that moved offshore would generate no revenue and no reduction in volatility [S3].
Economists disagree about whether speculation was the main driver of oil price swings; if other factors dominated, the tax would raise costs for traders without visibly lowering prices at the pump.
The bill did not estimate how much revenue the tax would raise, so the boost to the Highway Trust Fund is unquantified [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall mainly on speculative traders, while the potential benefits — steadier oil prices and new highway funding — reach ordinary consumers. The main design risk is that trading moves to offshore exchanges, shrinking both the revenue and the anti-speculation effect. On balance the bill's costs and benefits are reasonably aligned, though its revenue and price effects are unproven.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on July 29, 2009, with 29 additional cosponsors [S1] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the committee held no further action on it [S5].
No vote was ever taken in the House, and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil futures speculators and the exchanges that profit from high trading volume are better off because the tax never took effect; the Highway Trust Fund and drivers gained nothing.

for.name: Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 29 cosponsors.

for.name: 30 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including transportation committee leaders like Rep. Oberstar.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never took it up, marked it up, or reported it out.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; there is no record of Republican support, and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Democrat, so no vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Oil futures speculators and hedge funds
industries.note: The bill taxes every oil futures and options transaction, directly costing traders who buy and sell oil contracts without taking delivery. Ordinary drivers stand to gain from the calmer prices the tax is meant to produce.
Exchanges would be liable for collecting the tax on trades on their facilities, and reduced speculative volume would shrink their fee revenue.
Bona fide hedging transactions are exempt, so businesses locking in prices for real oil use avoid the tax while benefiting from less price volatility.
New revenue deposited into the Highway Trust Fund would flow to road and highway programs and the contractors that build them.
